articles.content:
About the Program

The Shadowing Program at NASA Glenn Research Center allows you to step behind the scenes and get a firsthand look at one of the world’s premier research facilities. Throughout the day, you will be paired with a NASA expert to explore state-of-the-art testing facilities and gain insight into what a career at NASA is like.

This opportunity is open to high school and college students, including students enrolled in vocational, technical, or trade schools, and community colleges. Applicants must be U.S. Citizens or Lawful Permanent Residents (Green Card Holders). More details on eligibility are found in the sections below. This program is only available in-person.

Dates for Skilled Trades, Engineering, and Business Shadowing Opportunities

  • March 18, 2027
  • April 22, 2027
  • May 20, 2027

2026-2027 Timeline

All dates are subject to change.

  • Oct. 23, 2026: Shadowing Applications Open
  • March 1, 2027: Shadowing Application Closes for the March 18 Shadowing Day
  • April 5, 2027: Shadowing Application Closes for the April 22 Shadowing Day
  • May 3, 2027: Shadowing Application Closes for the May 20 Shadowing Day

Note: Acceptance emails will be delivered two weeks prior to the shadowing date.

Eligibility

High school students must be at least 16 years old by their shadowing opportunity date and enrolled in their junior or senior year of high school. Students must be in good academic standing and interested in pursuing careers in aerospace including aerospace skilled trades.

Students ages 16-17 must enter a parent or guardian’s email address as part of the application process. An email will be sent to the parent or guardian’s email address with instructions for approving the student’s application.

To apply, please include the following:

  1. Download and fill out the appropriate Media Release Form and include as a Supporting Document (PDF or image) in your application submission on NASA STEM Gateway.
    • Media Release Form – under 18 years old
    • Media Release Form – 18 years or older
  2. Prepare a short essay (maximum 2500 characters, 12pt font) that describes why you want to participate in this shadowing experience. This essay should be uploaded as a Supporting Document (Word or PDF) in your application. The essay should address the following:
    • What career field are you interested in shadowing at NASA Glenn Research Center?
    • What would you like to achieve through participation in this program?
    • How would this opportunity impact your future?

      For this short essay, we want to hear your authentic voice. Please do not use Large Language Models (LLMs) or generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude) to write or draft your response. We are evaluating your genuine interest and personal goals, not the perfection of an AI-generated text.
  • Download the High School Shadowing  Acknowledgment Form. Your principal or counselor must sign the form to acknowledge your potential participation during school time. Include this file as a Supporting Document (PDF or image) in your application submission on NASA STEM Gateway.
    • High School Shadowing Principal-Counselor Acknowledgment Form

Links for the Shadowing Day opportunities are found below:

  • Skilled Trades – March 18, 2027 
  • Skilled Trades – April 22, 2027 
  • Skilled Trades – May 20, 2027 
  • Business & Management – March  18, 2027 
  • Business & Management – April 22, 2027 
  • Business & Management – May 20, 2027 
  • Engineering – March 18, 2027 
  • Engineering – April 22, 2027 
  • Engineering – May 20, 2027 

College students must be currently enrolled at an accredited college or university, including community colleges and technical or trade schools. Students must be in good academic standing and pursuing a degree or certification/licensure in at least one of the career areas listed below:

Skilled Trades: Electricians and Electronics, Welding, Fabrication, Machinist, Tool & Die, Instrumentation, Engineering Technicians and Computer/IT Technicians, and/or Cryogenics.

Engineering: Electrical Engineering, Electronics Engineering, Aerospace Engineering, Materials Engineering, Systems Engineering, or Nuclear Engineering.

Business: Management, Finance, or Accounting.

articles.author: Lee Mohon
articles.title: NASA Shares Plans to Accelerate Artemis, Return to Moon
articles.excerpt: In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.
articles.content:
In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.

Agency leadership provided updates on the previously announced acceleration plans for the Artemis program, advancing toward the agency’s Artemis III test flight in 2027 and Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028. Building on the priorities  announced at Ignition earlier this year, NASA leadership shared the agency’s significant progress across its missions, working with industry partners to test critical capabilities, reduce risk, and build toward a sustained American presence on the Moon.

“This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible,” said Isaacman. “NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we’re not waiting for others to bring their plans to us — the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth.”

The agency shared details of the Artemis III mission, which will test rendezvous, docking, and operations between NASA’s Orion spacecraft and lunar lander test vehicles from SpaceX and Blue Origin in Earth orbit. Four astronauts will fly aboard Orion, launched on NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit to reduce risk ahead of the Artemis IV moon landing mission.

The Artemis III mission will unfold in sequence: Blue Origin will launch a Blue Moon lander test article into Earth orbit, SLS will launch Orion and its crew, docking with the Blue Moon lander test article, then SpaceX will launch a Version 3 Starship lander test article while Orion will undock from Blue Moon and dock with Starship.

The Oct. 23 updates follow other recent updates about the Artemis missions. Hardware for Artemis III is on track, with processing timelines sharply reduced by about half. NASA also redesigned, built, and tested a critical fuel-line component in-house in five months, at roughly a tenth of the cost of an earlier outside-vendor estimate.

“NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it,” said Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager. “It’s an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise.”

Artemis IV: Pursuing multiple paths to Moon landing

For the agency’s Artemis IV mission in 2028, astronauts will launch aboard Orion on the SLS rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop lunar landers to carry those astronauts to the Moon’s surface. Both companies have redesigned their approaches to simplify the missions and make them more efficient and flexible as compared to previous mission designs.

SpaceX’s Starship will refuel in Earth orbit, rendezvous with Orion, and then carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Blue Origin’s approach involves transfer stages in Earth orbit to push its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander toward the Moon, where it will meet Orion in a closer lunar orbit before descending to the surface.

Both SpaceX and Blue Origin are targeting to be able to support a crewed lunar landing in 2028.  

For Artemis IV, NASA is pursuing two upper-stage options for the SLS rocket: its current stage, the interim cryogenic propulsion stage; and a stretched version of ULA’s Centaur V which can carry more propellant. Pursuing both options ensures NASA is maintaining flexibility and preventing single-point dependency.

NASA also announced plans with spacesuit provider Axiom Space to develop a second, lighter suit design called the “Sortie suit” to enable the first moonwalks. The Sortie suit will not replace Axiom’s primary suit, which will be used for longer, more demanding missions in the future. The Sortie suit is roughly half the weight of the larger suit and lets NASA move faster on the earliest surface missions.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions at the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.
Learn more about Artemis:

https://www.nasa.gov/artemis

articles.author: Andrew Crocker
articles.title: We’re Asking the Ninth Circuit to Hold Reverse Location Warrants Categorically Unconstitutional
articles.excerpt: Yesterday, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Ninth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Spurlock, a case involving a “tower dump” warrant. These overbroad warrants require cellular providers to turn over location data about every phone in a given area at a given time. This is the first such case to be heard by a federal appeals court since the US Supreme Court ruled this summer that highly similar “geofence” warrants are searches under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.
articles.content:
Andrew Crocker · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

Yesterday, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Ninth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Spurlock, a case involving a “tower dump” warrant. These overbroad warrants require cellular providers to turn over location data about every phone in a given area at a given time. This is the first such case to be heard by a federal appeals court since the US Supreme Court ruled this summer that highly similar “geofence” warrants are searches under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Spurlock involves an investigation into two murder victims discovered on the side of a rural California highway. Police also found a car belonging to one of the victims several miles away on the same highway. They quickly sought a tower dump warrant for an area covering this stretch of road, which eventually revealed location data on nearly 1,700 unique phones. Faced with a motion to suppress, the district court relied on a Fifth Circuit court of appeals decision about geofence warrants to hold that tower dumps are similarly categorically unconstitutional “general warrants” that violate the Fourth Amendment. However, the court refused to suppress evidence on the basis of the “good faith doctrine.”

Our amicus brief on appeal makes several key arguments.

First, we point out that the Supreme Court’s decision in the geofence case Chatrie v. United States this summer only strengthens the arguments that tower dumps are unconstitutional general warrants. Tower dumps are a somewhat older technique than geofence warrants, but they are both “reverse location searches,” in which police “tap into an all-encompassing database, allowing them to undertake nearly perfect, retrospective surveillance of countless persons and places.” This is the sort of untargeted “general warrant” the framers of the Fourth Amendment wanted to prevent. As we write in the brief, “Searching all people in an area without probable cause to believe they were all involved in the criminal activity under investigation reproduces the evils of general warrants and is not constitutionally permitted.” It’s this rule of law that prevents police from searching the houses of a hundred, or even a thousand people in the vicinity of a crime.

Second, we note that even if high courts continue to allow tower dump and geofence warrants in any cases, core Fourth Amendment law requires strict limits to protect the privacy of innocent bystanders, including limits on the scope and duration of the warrants, as well notice to affected individuals and after-the-fact deletion and minimization of irrelevant data.

Finally, we argue that the Fourth Amendment requires the court to set aside the good faith doctrine in cases like these and actually decide the constitutional issue. Too often courts pass the buck in cases involving novel surveillance techniques, leading to situations where police can continue using the technique for years or even decades without a definitive ruling.

articles.author: Katharine Trendacosta
articles.title: Google Summaries Aren't About AI, They're About Lock-In
articles.excerpt: Whether they call it AI summaries, knowledge panels, or AMP, Google takes actions that are less about functionality and more about locking you into its own ecosystem. Knowing that makes it possible for all of us to choose better services than Google's, defeating their anticompetitive goal. In this case, as it is so often, knowledge is power.
articles.content:
Katharine Trendacosta · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

Whether they call it AI summaries, knowledge panels, or AMP, Google takes actions that are less about functionality and more about locking you into its own ecosystem. Knowing that makes it possible for all of us to choose better services than Google's, defeating their anticompetitive goal. In this case, as it is so often, knowledge is power.  

In the old days, when dinosaurs roamed the earth and getting online involved your computer making eldritch shrieking, Google was a website that took whatever you typed in and gave you a list of links that best matched what you were searching for. As it's grown beyond that, however, the core function of Google Search has moved from giving you the best answer to your query to a number of other things, most of them about making money for Google. 

This is obviously not a new observation. It's at the core of what EFF Special Advisor Cory Doctorow named "enshittification." But it's important to remember that whatever shiny new name or technology is wrapped around these tools, it's not about the wrapping, it's about the monetization. 

In the case of Google Search, the company has a history of rolling out new "features" that are less helpful to the searcher and more designed to keep you and your data within the Google ecosystem. One easy example of enshittification is putting sponsored links and ads at the top of search results, forcing you to scroll down past a bunch of not relevant links to get to your answers. Or, in some cases, accidentally clicking on sponsored links that might be designed to give you the opposite information of what you're looking for or for a competitor to the product you intended to buy.  

The other clumsy version of this is Google's self-preferencing, where Google's own services—say YouTube if you're looking for a video—are weighted so that they appear at the top of a search over a competitor's. Similar to this was Google's push for websites, particularly news ones, to be made available via what it called "Accelerated Mobile Pages" or AMP, which in theory stripped out features that might make loading a page on mobile too slow, but also handed over control of how webpages looked on mobile to Google and turned mobile links, often by default, into Google links.  

But the other way that Google has historically kept your—and your valuable eyeballs—on its website has been to just obviate the need to even click on a link and leave Google at all. The first version of this was what Google calls "knowledge panels." These are snippets of information shown on the results page of a search that purport to answer your question. Knowledge panels predate the AI push and haven't always been what you could call accurate.  

Knowledge panels are extremely similar to the AI summaries we now see at the top of Google Search results, except that instead of pulling quotes from specific linked sources, it's the AI doing the summarizing, though also sometimes with links. They are basically the same thing, mostly changed only in branding, because AI is now the cool kid on the block. The goal is essentially the same—it's less about providing you with the best answer to your query and more about making you think it's unnecessary to click a link and leave Google's ecosystem. And, more importantly, it keeps you on Google's pages longer to read the content. More time on the page is more time exposed to ads and sponsored links and more money for Google.  

The biggest irony here is that it didn’t even work. People choosing to use “AI mode”—and possibly made accustomed to getting information as text instead of links through the knowledge panels and the AI summaries at the top—has caused “lower monetization” via ads. Ads, remember, are Google’s main source of revenue. Like newspapers before them, Google is finding that counting on a monopoly on ad space maybe isn’t the most sound strategy in a shifting technological landscape. And to get out of the hole it has made for itself, it is lighting cash on fire to try to get back on top. Perhaps they should consider pivoting to video.  

Every time you see a feature like this, no matter what it is called or what "new" technology they claim fuels it, remember that it is Google's monetary incentives that drive the decisions and not necessarily the tech itself. And you can always choose to ignore it, scroll past, disable it, or even go to another service entirely.

The castle we see today dates principally from the late medieval period. articles.author: Jessica Taveau
articles.title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
articles.excerpt: NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems.
articles.content:
NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems.

Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace.

The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029.

The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are:

  • Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million.
  • Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million.
  • Viasat Inc. for $460.9 million.

Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services.

To learn more about NASA’s Network Extension for User Continuity and Sustainability Ka-band service acquisition, visit:

https://go.nasa.gov/4iVfeVB

-end-

Jennifer Dooren / Jessica Taveau

articles.author: Global Voices Brazil
articles.title: The scandals and suspects surrounding Flávio Bolsonaro, according to the Brazilian press
articles.excerpt: After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family
articles.content:
This story by Global Voices Brazil originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family

Forty-eight hours after losing the runoff in Brazil to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro, former president Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, a senator representing Rio de Janeiro, fled to the United States. From there, where his brother Eduardo, a former congressman, has lived since February 2025, he continues to challenge the results of the election he lost by 4.4 million votes, as attested by the Electoral Court (TSE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and other right-led governments in the region.

Upon landing in Miami, Flávio published a letter proclaiming himself “the true president of Brazil” and “president-elect of Brazil.” After 22 minutes — and a demand from the US Department of State — he retracted to “the leader of Brazil.”

US President Donald Trump had said that Brazil’s elections “looked rigged,” but he wouldn't “get involved.” The New York Times reported, however, that Flávio was helped by Trump's aides. “The jet [he traveled on] had been arranged by a White House official,” affirmed the newspaper.

Flávio’s narrative is that he is being persecuted by the Brazilian justice system and Lula’s government as an opposition leader, since the Supreme Court ordered the seizure of his passports — he also has Italian citizenship — right after his defeat was announced.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, considered a foe of the Bolsonaro family and himself under suspicion for having links to the same disgraced banker connected to Flávio, issued the order in response to a Federal Police request that considered Flávio a flight risk. In Brazil, a president cannot be investigated for alleged crimes committed before their term, meaning that once elected, all pending investigations involving Flávio would have been suspended. This is also the first time in 24 years that Flávio will not have a seat to ensure his parliamentary immunity.

According to the Brazilian Federal Police, three elements indicated a flight risk in Flávio’s case: an interview his brother Eduardo gave to a podcast in the US defending the idea of him leaving the country, on October 23, his considerable economic power, and well-established structures abroad that could support him in a long stay.

The day after the election, after visiting his father, who is under house arrest convicted for a coup attempt, Flávio recorded a video complaining about the measure, claiming “he never thought about leaving the country” and promising to stay and answer to investigations. Overnight, apparently, he had a change of heart in time for a new plan.

Investigations and corruption suspicions have long surrounded his name. In 2020, Sergio Moro, the judge who convicted Lula, resigned as Bolsonaro’s justice minister, accusing the president of trying to intervene with the Federal Police to protect Flávio in an embezzlement and money-laundering inquiry. In a cabinet meeting, then-president Bolsonaro shouted at his ministers: “I won’t wait until they fuck my entire family,” saying he would fire whoever got in their way.

During this election campaign, skeletons in Flávio's closet were further exposed in stories published by the Brazilian press. Global Voices gathered the main ones here. Flávio is currently under three investigations at the Supreme Court.

Rachadinha

This is the case that led Jair Bolsonaro to allegedly interfere in the Federal Police in 2020. Flávio was indicted by Rio’s Public Prosecution Office for embezzlement, money laundering, and criminal organization. The case was later adjourned. Rachadinha (“split” in English) is a salary kickback scheme in which a politician hires someone for a certain position and then reclaims part of their salary.

In 2018, after Bolsonaro’s election, a report by the Council for Financial Activities Control (Coaf) pointed to atypical financial movements in the account of Flávio’s aide, Fabricio Queiroz, an old friend of his father. Queiroz, who was filmed paying for Flávio's daughters’ tuition in cash, was identified as the scheme’s operator. For the Public Prosecution Office, according to UOL news outlet, the scheme was used to cover Flávio’s personal expenses and to increase his patrimony.

There were also suspicions that a chocolate franchise shop, owned by Flávio, was used for money laundering. The investigation found 1,512 cash deposits in repeated amounts between March 2015 and December 2018 at the establishment.

An audio recording found by police in 2024 shows then-president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s attorneys, and Alexandre Ramagem, former director of the Brazilian Intelligence Agency (Abin), currently a fugitive living in the US, allegedly discussing a plan to free Flávio from the investigations through Federal Revenue Service employees.

‘Dark Horse’ and Vorcaro

On May 13, 2026, The Intercept Brasil published a story and an audio recording showing that the movie “Dark Horse,” a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro, starring Jim Caviezel, could have been financed by disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro. Before the story went out, a reporter from the news outlet asked Flávio about the case. The senator laughed and dismissed the question, saying: “That’s a lie! Where did you get this from?”

Vorcaro is at the center of one of the country's biggest scandals, involving politicians, members of the Supreme Court and other judges, and celebrities, through his bank, Master — its license was approved during Jair Bolsonaro’s government. Vorcaro is investigated for a fraud scheme that caused a BRL 47 billion (around USD 8.7 billion) loss to the Credit Guarantee Fund (FGC), which backs Brazil's banking system.

The messages published by The Intercept show Flávio negotiating with Vorcaro on WhatsApp. Flávio asked for BRL 134 million (USD 24.9 million) and received at least BRL 61 million (USD 11.17 million). In one of the last messages between them, before Vorcaro was arrested while trying to flee the country, Flávio tells him: “Brother, I am and will always be with you; there is no half-talk between us,” reported TIB.

Since he couldn’t deny their link, Flávio has repeated that the money he negotiated with Vorcaro was “private money for a private movie.”

This is also one of the investigations into Flávio at the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which targets the movie’s financing operation. Despite the movie being filmed in Brazil, Vorcaro sent the money to a fund in the US (Havengate), managed by a friend of Eduardo Bolsonaro’s. The final destination for the money hasn't been confirmed yet.

Willer Thomaz, a friend 

Another inquiry investigates Flávio for money laundering and currency evasion, along with his friend Willer Tomaz, a Brazilian lawyer also currently in the US. Tomaz is under investigation for money laundering through betting companies and involvement in another scandal, a fraud scheme at the national pension fund (INSS).

Documents accessed by Brazilian news outlets showed that Tomaz alone moved BRL 5 billion (around USD 930 million) in betting sites and cashed out BRL 200 million (USD 37.2 million).

When Piauí magazine revealed that Flávio had travelled in Vorcaro’s plane with his family, the senator’s first reaction was to say that “fortunately, it was Willer's.” His friend shared the plane’s quotas with a Vorcaro company. Tomaz denied ever meeting with the banker.

In October, O Globo newspaper published that Flávio had been registered as a “master user” on an offshore account under the name of a company managed by Tomaz and registered on Madeira Island, Portugal. This status could give him “significant operational access,” according to the Federal Police. Piauí magazine also says the senator could have been an indirect partner in a betting company based in São Paulo, but controlled by another company registered in Madeira, also linked to Tomaz. Flávio denies it.

Folha de S. Paulo newspaper says that the relationship between Flávio and Tomaz began in 2019. During the COVID-19 parliamentary inquiry commission at the National Congress, two years later, the senator defended Tomaz, calling him a friend. They always denied being business associates, claiming they were only friends.

Ana Clara’s death and the militias 

On the morning of February 2, 2021, five-year-old Ana Clara Machado was shot and killed while playing at the doorstep of her home, in Rio de Janeiro. The Military Police denied any confrontation or the presence of narcos in the area where their operation was taking place. Later, the Civil Police identified police officer Bruno Delaroli as the shooter and arrested him. In March, 2026, ICL Notícias, a news website, reported that Flávio Bolsonaro worked on the officer's defense team in the higher courts, trying to avoid a jury trial. Another news outlet, UOL, revealed he worked pro bono. Lula questioned the senator about his motives during a debate on TV Globo.

Also, according to ICL, this wasn’t the only case Flávio advocated for officers accused of killings. Folha says his career as a defense lawyer gained traction after he was elected senator.

During his political life, Flávio has had a long history of links to police officers identified as members of so-called militias — paramilitary groups mostly formed by active and retired officers, carrying out vigilante and organized crime activities in dominated territories. When a state deputy in Rio, Flávio employed at his office the mother and wife of Adriano da Nobrega, an ex-military policeman, linked to a militia known as Crime Office, whose main activities were to execute ordered killings. He also sent parliamentary money to an NGO connected to another police officer involved in the murder of Rio’s city councillor Marielle Franco. According to Piauí magazine, the militia man known as “Peixe” (fish) referred to Flávio as “our senator.”

ICL News says the UN will examine Flávio's links to the militias when analyzing Ana Clara’s case.

Written by Global Voices Brazil

articles.content:
Sean Gregory is the project manager for NASA’s Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) Management Office within the SNWG implementation team. Gregory manages more than 20 SNWG projects that meet Earth observation needs for federal agencies, including Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 and Observation Products for End-Users for Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA). 

Prior to joining the Office of Data Science and Informatics team at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, Gregory was the chief safety and mission assurance officer for the SLS (Space Launch System) boosters, where he oversaw quality, reliability, and systems safety activities for the boosters and supported the Artemis I launch. Gregory received a Space Flight Awareness Silver Snoopy Award for his work on the SLS boosters. He also led the operations team and the reliability and maintainability team within the Safety and Mission Assurance Program Analysis and Systems Integration Group. 

Gregory holds bachelor’s degrees in engineering physics and economics from West Virginia Wesleyan College and a master’s degree in mechanical engineering from West Virginia University.

articles.content:
Dr. Pontus Olofsson is a research scientist at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where he leads the agency’s contribution to the interagency Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) through NASA’s SNWG Implementation Team, known as NSITE. Through the working group, NSITE identifies, communicates, and addresses the Earth observation needs of federal agencies to support their ongoing missions and applications. This work has resulted in some of NASA’s most impactful data products, including the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 dataset, which has distributed more than 6 billion files. 

Prior to joining NASA in 2022, Olofsson was a research professor in the Department of Earth and Environment at Boston University. He completed his academic training at Lund University in Sweden, earning degrees in physical geography and mathematical statistics, followed by a doctorate in physical geography in 2007. 

Olofsson’s primary research focuses on mining archives of satellite data to understand Earth’s changes and their impact on people and the environment. He has a special interest in combining remote sensing data and statistical sampling techniques to measure environmental change.

articles.title: Manil Maskey
articles.excerpt: Dr. Manil Maskey is a manager and senior research scientist at NASA, specializing in data science, including superintelligence, data systems and visualization. He leads the Office of Data Science and Informatics at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where he drives advanced super intelligence (SI) tools and digital transformation initiatives across scientific domains.
articles.content:
Dr. Manil Maskey is a manager and senior research scientist at NASA, specializing in data science, including superintelligence, data systems and visualization. He leads the Office of Data Science and Informatics at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where he drives advanced super intelligence (SI) tools and digital transformation initiatives across scientific domains. 

Maskey holds a Bachelor of Science in computer science and mathematics, as well as a Master of Science and a doctorate in computer science, with research focused on high-dimensional data visualization and machine learning. Over a 25-year career, his work has spanned industry, academia and government. He began as a software engineer at NCR/Teradata before spending 12 years as a research scientist at the University of Alabama in Huntsville. 

At NASA, Maskey has spearheaded key programs and projects, including the Visualization, Exploration, and Data Analysis (VEDA) data platform, the Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program’s data management project, and major cloud migration efforts. During a detail at NASA Headquarters in Washington, he served as the data science and innovation lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer, shaping the NASA Science Mission Directorate’s overall SI strategy and promoting ethical SI principles across scientific disciplines. 

He represents NASA nationally as a steering committee member for the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource and co-chair of the Networking and Information Technology Research and Development Big Data Interagency Working Group. Additionally, Maskey is an adjunct professor at UAH, a senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), and chair of the IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Society Earth Science Informatics Technical Committee. 

His contributions to NASA have earned him numerous honors, including the NASA Silver Achievement Medal, the NASA Exceptional Achievement Medal, several innovation awards, and multiple Group Achievement Awards.

articles.content:
Kaylin Bugbee leads the information management focus area within the Office of Data Science and Informatics at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. She manages a portfolio of projects aimed at making NASA’s scientific data systems and information resources more discoverable, resilient, and efficient while enabling open science through transparency, reproducibility, and open access. Her portfolio includes the Science Discovery Engine, the NASA Science Research Data Repository, and the Science Mission Directorate Governance initiative. 

Together, these projects form the Data and Analysis Services Project, also led by Bugbee and managed by NASA’s Office of the Chief Science Data Officer. Her efforts to generate, repair, improve, care for, document, and update NASA’s science data ensure it is available today and for future scientists and decision-makers. 

Bugbee holds Bachelor of Arts degrees in philosophy and English, a Bachelor of Science in Earth system science, and a Master of Arts in Earth system science from the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH). Prior to joining NASA in 2020, she supported the Earth Science Data System while working as a research associate at UAH. She has contributed to several high-impact initiatives, including the Climate Data Initiative and a metadata quality review of more than 7,000 Earth science metadata records. 

Bugbee also worked with the Global Hydrometeorology Resource Center Distributed Active Archive Center and has supported activities within NASA’s Interagency Implementation and Advanced Concepts Team. These include the Analysis and Review of the Common Metadata Repository, the Multi-Mission Algorithm and Analysis Platform, the Algorithm Publication Tool, and the Data Curation for Discovery project.

articles.excerpt: David Meyer is the deputy manager of the Office of Data Science and Informatics at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Meyer provides supervision and strategic direction for the office’s development of science informatics and cloud solutions during a period of rapid growth and change.
articles.content:
David Meyer is the deputy manager of the Office of Data Science and Informatics at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Meyer provides supervision and strategic direction for the office’s development of science informatics and cloud solutions during a period of rapid growth and change. 

He interfaces with and supports customers at NASA Headquarters and within several NASA organizations, including the Earth Science Division, the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer, the Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program, the Earth Action Program, the Disasters Program, and the Earth Science Data and Information System Project. 

Previously, Meyer was a member of the Chandra X-ray Observatory High Resolution Mirror Assembly Test Team and served in project offices, including the X-37 Project Office, the Space Shuttle Program’s Redesigned Solid Rocket Motor Project Office, and the SLS (Space Launch System) Booster Element Office. Meyer brings more than 20 years of human spaceflight experience, along with 15 years of supervisory experience leading high-performing teams in the Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate and Science and Technology Office at Marshall. 

Meyer’s leadership has been recognized with numerous awards, including NASA’s Outstanding Leadership Medal, Silver Achievement Medal, and recognition as a Space Flight Awareness Honoree.

articles.content:
Elizabeth Fancher is a project manager at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where she leads project formulation and implementation activities. She ensures alignment with project requirements while managing documentation, budget development, procurement planning, and resource distribution across the Office of Data Science and Informatics. 

In her role, Fancher supports the Data and Analysis Services Project and serves as the public-private partnership lead, overseeing the development of Space Act Agreements in collaboration with the NASA Partnership Office. 

Before joining NASA, Fancher was lead project coordinator for the NASA Interagency Implementation and Advanced Concepts Team (IMPACT), operating as product owner and Scrum Master. In this capacity, she facilitated Agile planning, coordinated resources and risks, managed action tracking, and supported technical interchange and communication across interagency partners. Her background also includes leadership roles in recruiting and customer service, bringing a foundation in workforce coordination, team development, and stakeholder engagement. 

Fancher earned a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Mississippi and holds certifications as a Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) Scrum Master and SAFe Product Owner/Product Manager. She has received multiple awards for her leadership, collaboration, and contributions to NASA’s science and technology initiatives.

articles.content:
Dr. Brian Freitag leads the Data Systems Evolution team in the Office of Data Science and Informatics at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. In this role, he enables scientific exploration and discovery through data visualization techniques and analysis capabilities that lower the barrier to entry for cloud-hosted data. 

Freitag oversees major initiatives including the Visualization, Exploration, and Data Analysis (VEDA) project, which promotes data interoperability and incorporates an open-source science cyberinfrastructure. Prior to VEDA, he led the production of NASA’s Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 dataset distributed by the Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center and managed petabyte-scale projects with industry partners. 

Since joining NASA in September 2020, Freitag’s leadership and contributions to cloud-based Earth science research platforms have earned multiple NASA Group Achievement Awards. His expertise spans machine learning forecasting applications, disaster monitoring, and large-scale data production. He holds a doctorate and a master’s degree in atmospheric science from the University of Alabama in Huntsville, as well as a master’s degree in Earth and planetary science. His dedication to open science and data-driven storytelling continues to accelerate discovery and propel the next generation of scientific researchers.

articles.author: Dede Dinius
articles.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
articles.excerpt: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets.
articles.content:
NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets.

An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California.

During the tests, the SPLICE payload used an advanced guidance system to map the terrain and assess potential landing areas. If the system determines the targeted landing area is unsafe, the system diverts the drone to a safer location. The system generates high-resolution digital elevation maps from light-detection and sensor data.

Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed the SPLICE payload and partnered with specialists at NASA Armstrong to integrate, test, and fly it aboard the Alta-X drone in June and July. Those tests verified communications, data handling, telemetry, and command- control performance between the SPLICE payload and the drone to prepare for a full-scale test at Voyager Technologies in Mojave, California, later this month.

“This flight test is the culmination of almost a decade of work, for the SPLICE project,” said Davis Adams, NASA project manager. “This flight raised the technology readiness level, priming it for integration into future robotic and crewed lunar flights. Validation of the guidance and navigation systems are applicable to terrestrial, lunar, and Martian descent and landing missions.”

NASA has worked with a number of commercial lunar lander providers to implement iterations of SPLICE into their platforms. A number of the landers slated for upcoming Moon Base missions leverage data collected by NASA through the development of systems like SPLICE to execute soft touchdowns on the lunar surface.

“We are coordinating with industry regarding the usage of the guidance system once the system is available in the NASA software catalog, currently planned for this fall,” Adams said. “Some of the companies also are  evaluating the system’s navigation capabilities for precision landing applications, as well as potential extensions for autonomous surface mobility.”

NASA’s Flight Opportunities project, based at NASA Armstrong, enabled flight testing of the SPLICE project early in its development that laid a foundation for it to continue advancing its technology readiness level to what it is today. Flight testing included both a descent altitude and a landing trajectory in 2019 similar to what is expected on a lunar mission and the demonstration of two NASA-developed precision landing sensor systems in 2020.

articles.author: Sandra May
articles.title: NASA Space Grant Students Fuel Agency’s Inspiration Tour
articles.excerpt: NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. At nearly every stop across the country, NASA Space Grant has brought students into the heart of the action.
articles.content:
NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. At nearly every stop across the country, NASA Space Grant has brought students into the heart of the action.

In Iowa, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman toured the Make to Innovate program lab at Iowa State University. Students from the Iowa Space Grant Consortium’s Mission Moon program, along with consortium-funded student organizations including Cardinal Space Mining, CySat, and CyLaunch, shared research findings and demonstrated the institution’s strong connection to NASA via agency-funded projects. During a well-attended town hall event NASA experts briefed students on the agency’s Moon Base efforts and how their work can contribute to future exploration.

“We’re grateful for the opportunity to welcome NASA leadership to Iowa State,” said Sara Nelson Iowa Space Grant director. “The excitement among students was incredible, and the visit highlighted how the research and innovation happening in Iowa can help advance Artemis and NASA’s future exploration efforts.”

At the University of Arizona, the NASA administrator saw firsthand the space research and engineering capabilities that are enabled by the Arizona Space Grant Consortium. From satellite communications testing to complex optics for peering into deep space to student-built high-altitude balloon payloads and even small satellites, students at the University of Arizona have a long history of contributing to NASA missions and making aerospace career connections. This tour stop also included a Q&A session where the NASA administrator answered questions from local high school and college students.

“It was incredible to present the high-altitude ballooning research we do in SEDS (Students for the Exploration and Development of Space) to Jared Isaacman and those at NASA,” said Ella Miller, a junior studying mechanical engineering at the University of Arizona. “Arizona Space Grant has allowed me to get hands-on experience through an entire mission design process every semester, helping me pursue a career in space research and secure internships in this field.”

At the University of Alaska in Fairbanks, the Administrator toured two Geophysical Institute facilities: Poker Flat Research Range, the university’s scientific rocket launching facility, and the Alaska Satellite Facility. During an Alaska Space Grant science fair, students shared research in hibernation biology and showcased CubeSat technology advancements. Students were also able to learn about the agency’s Moon Base program and ask questions about opportunities available to the next generation of innovators and explorers.

In North Dakota, the Inspiration Tour focused on future exploration capabilities. Space Grant-funded research at the University of North Dakota is helping to shape the future of exploration across STEM fields. Student fellows and NASA interns shared their projects on supercell mergers using satellite imagery, geomagnetic conditions of aurora borealis, and in-situ resource utilization, to name a few. North Dakota Space Grant STEM ambassador students also shared robotics and drone activities as part of “Mission Moon”, which centers Artemis initiatives in statewide collaborations with educators and other North Dakota colleges and universities.

“Getting to speak with the NASA Administrator was an amazing opportunity!” said research fellow and STEM ambassador Malissa Reinhardt. “He genuinely cared about what we students had to say and the research we’re working on, which makes all the hard work we put into our research and North Dakota Space Grant Consortium so rewarding.”

NASA’s Inspiration Tour will culminate in MAX POWER, a public showcase of air and space innovation on Nov. 7 and 8, highlighting the agency’s commitment to preparing the next generation of innovators and explorers for humanity’s next giant leap. As NASA enters a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, the national network of Space Grant consortia is expanding opportunities for students to lead the way in an aerospace workforce that is evolving and growing. At learning institutions from coast to coast, today’s Space Grant students are launching America’s future in space.

To find ways to engage with NASA’s exciting missions, broad range of careers, and unique learning opportunities, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/learning-resources

articles.author: Zulker Naeen
articles.title: Tracing the recruitment trap behind Russia’s war
articles.excerpt: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
articles.content:
This story by Zulker Naeen originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war

Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.

What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine. He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.

His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.

A war that is running out of men

Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.

Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries. Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.

One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.

Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.

Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.

Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.

Who is accepting this offer?

Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation (ORF). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.

Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.

But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted, while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy. Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds. Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.

The legal door and the missing agreement

Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training (BMET) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe; the private market carried the rest.

However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.

The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.

Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).

Agents, agencies, and the price of a seat

The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.

Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.

Counting the dead without a count

Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.

These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.

Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.

No Justice for the victims

Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.

In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.

Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.

Written by Zulker Naeen

articles.content: Explanation: “I see” IC 342, the Hidden Galaxy! Today’s image peers through the plane of the Milky Way, through all its gas, dust and stars, to unveil this spiral galaxy. IC 342 (or Caldwell 5) is one of the brightest members of the IC 342/Maffei group of galaxies. Located about 10 million light years away, this group is quite close to the Local Group that includes our Milky Way. Inaccurate accounting of the crowded and dusty Milky Way foreground has led to misunderstandings in IC 342’s history, including the theory that the galaxy was ejected from the Local Group. IC 342 has its own dust intermittently blocking the glow of hydrogen gas, indicating the presence of bright, young stars. Magnetic field maps of IC 342 reveal that magnetic fields may contribute substantially to one of the biggest galactic puzzles: how do spiral arms form?

articles.title: Before the Dawn in America’s Heartland
articles.excerpt: The predawn hours brought clear skies over much of the eastern United States on October 18, 2026. An astronaut aboard the International Space Station seized the opportunity to capture this wide-angle photo at 4:54 a.m. Central Daylight Time (09:54 Universal Time), with illuminated cities large and small arrayed across the darkened landscape.
articles.content:
The predawn hours brought clear skies over much of the eastern United States on October 18, 2026. An astronaut aboard the International Space Station seized the opportunity to capture this wide-angle photo at 4:54 a.m. Central Daylight Time (09:54 Universal Time), with illuminated cities large and small arrayed across the darkened landscape.

The U.S. Midwest’s largest metropolitan areas, such as Chicago, Illinois, and Detroit, Michigan, stand out as some of the brightest features. Mid-sized cities—including Indianapolis, Indiana; Cincinnati, Ohio; and Louisville, Kentucky—and their interconnections along state and interstate highways also shine brightly.

Above the web of nighttime lights and Earth’s lower atmosphere, a diffuse layer of green and orange is visible along the horizon to the left. This band of light is airglow, produced when sunlight strikes atoms and molecules in the upper atmosphere and causes them to eject photons. To the right, light from the Sun arcs across the horizon; sunrise was about an hour away on the East Coast and about two hours away in Chicago.

Astronaut photos and other remote sensing observations of nighttime lights are scientifically valuable for tracking changes in the built environment. For example, Chicago’s lightscape appears a homogeneous pale yellow in the wide view above. But in detailed photos, like the one below, a range of colors stemming from different types of lighting is discernible. Using NASA’s extensive Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth archive, researchers have developed a method for distinguishing lighting types within the pixels of nighttime photos. Systematically quantifying urban lights’ brightness, color, and extent can provide insight into how cities grow and evolve.

Satellite sensors also observe changes to lighting. In particular, NASA’s Black Marble nighttime lights product suite uses satellite observations to produce science-quality records of nighttime lights across the globe at daily, monthly, and yearly time scales. In the eastern U.S., scientists have used these data to track everything from power outages and restoration following major storms to lighting changes associated with new infrastructure to transitions to LED lighting from older forms.

Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-226709 was acquired on October 18, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 14 millimeters, and photograph ISS070-E-105097 was acquired on March 1, 2024, with a Nikon D5 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. They are provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The images were taken by members of the Expedition 75 and Expedition 70 crews, respectively. The images have been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

References & Resources

  • NASA Earth Observatory (2026, May 15) Picturing Earth in a New Light. Accessed November 3, 2026.
  • NASA Earth Observatory (2024, November 24) Windy City of Lights. Accessed November 3, 2026.
  • NASA Earth Observatory (2017, December 27) Observing Changes in Nighttime Lights. Accessed November 3, 2026.

articles.author: Aaron Mackey
articles.title: Postal Service Surveilled Protest Activities Online With Little Rules, Oversight
articles.excerpt: The U.S. Postal Service used social media surveillance to monitor and report on protests across the political spectrum, government records show.
articles.content:
Aaron Mackey · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

The U.S. Postal Service used social media surveillance to monitor and report on protests across the political spectrum, government records show.

The records, disclosed to EFF and other requesters suing the postal service under the Freedom of Information Act, show that the agency’s internet Covert Operations Program, or iCOP, routinely sifted through social media posts organizing and discussing protests with little records of any oversight or legal justification.

EFF filed suit in 2021 after Yahoo News disclosed the program’s existence and how the agency used it to monitor First Amendment protected activities. After years of delays and technical failures that led the agency to lose access to a trove of emails discussing the program, the postal service disclosed records to EFF and several other requesters this year.

The Postal Service used iCOP to surveil First Amendment activities

The disclosures include a series of bulletins created from iCOP, which show that the postal service used the program in 2020 and 2021 to monitor and circulate information about a wide range of planned protests. They included a planned “Million MAGA March,” a guns rights advocacy event and counter-protest in Virginia, a nationwide Save the Post Office Saturday protest, and planned protests in front of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy’s home in Washington, D.C.

Many of the bulletins provide dry descriptions of the events being planned and reference public discussions or events on major social media services. Others seem to imply or anticipate that the protests would turn violent.

For example, in discussing planned national and international protests scheduled for March 20, 2021, the bulletin references potential violence in light of “online inflammatory material.” Yet the bulletin acknowledges that the agency has “no intelligence to suggest specific threats.” This bulletin was described by Yahoo News when it disclosed iCOP’s existence.

Another bulletin discussing an ongoing Black Lives Matter protests in response to police shooting and killing people styles itself as a “National Civil Unrest Update.” The bulletins also recount and monitor threats sent to then-Postmaster DeJoy.

The Postal Service also disclosed three email chains to EFF that, while heavily redacted, show how the agency queried iCOP and disseminated what it found (Read the emails here, here, and here). The government agreed to release the email messages as part of settling EFF’s FOIA suit this fall. To EFF’s knowledge, they are the only existing materials that reflect how the agency queried iCOP.

Postal Service renames iCOP and loses access to records about it

According to the agency, after Yahoo News disclosed the program in 2021, the postal service renamed it and publicly said that it had stopped issuing bulletins. But the documents do not say that the agency’s social media surveillance stopped.

At the same time, EFF and several other FOIA requesters sought records detailing how the agency used iCOP and what rules the postal service had for using the program and distributing information it gained from surveilling social media. EFF spent years pushing the agency to disclose email communications about the program, which the agency had stored on an external hard drive. Amid these negotiations, someone dropped the hard drive, rendering it inoperable, agency officials said. By the time that happened, the agency had already deleted the underlying email messages pursuant to the agency’s retention schedule.

Minimal records disclosed about internal limits on surveillance programs

EFF’s FOIA request sought internal rules, guidance, and training that would show what safeguard the Postal Service imposed to protect First Amendment rights. The agency disclosed very few documents in response to this part of EFF’s request.

For example, a series of slides give an overview of the program, but do not explain how officials used iCOP. The closest thing to internal guideline that the agency disclosed were talking points the Chief Postal Inspector authored in response to questions about iCOP.

The inspector wrote that, “In reviewing social media postings to gather information we did not single out any particular group and did not base what was reviewed on race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, immigration status, or a person’s exercise of First Amendment freedoms.” The statement echoes language in the bulletin stating that its purpose is not to infringe on First Amendment rights; Other parts of the talking points characterize the surveillance as providing officials with situational awareness.

The postal inspector’s talking points go on to say that “the recent attention on iCOP has highlighted opportunities for improvement, including enhanced executive oversight. We have stopped the distribution of the bulletins like the one you have seen in the media reports.”

Setting aside that it’s unclear whether internal oversight occurred or resulted in any changes, the claim that iCOP did not infringe on First Amendment rights rings hollow. As the records disclosed show, surveilling and reporting on social media users’ efforts to organize rallies and protests was a feature of iCOP.

But more fundamentally, the claims by Postal Service officials fail to recognize that surveillance directly chills First Amendment rights. Further, the government can misuse the information it obtained as part of its social media surveillance to harass or retaliate against those exercising their constitutional rights.

Although EFF’s case seeking records about iCOP has ended, we will continue to bring more transparency to the government’s use of social media surveillance and look for ways to challenge the practice, especially when people are caught in the dragnet for exercising the First Amendment rights.

Related Cases:  EFF v. USPS - Social media monitoring (iCOP)
